title: Enquiry opened
body:
At 08:40 this morning, Head Office emailed the editor to ask for a festive photo of “the team enjoying the Communal Tin” for the Christmas newsletter. At 08:41 the editor discovered he had no idea where the Communal Tin was.

The tin, which is round, tartan and full of Assorted Shortbread, was posted to him in February with the instruction “please share with the team”. The team is spread across three countries, so the editor put it somewhere very safe while he drafted a Sharing Framework. The Framework is on draft four and runs to nine pages, one of which is a flowchart. The tin has not been seen since the spring.

An enquiry has been opened. The editor has appointed himself Senior Investigating Officer, after a rigorous selection process in which he was the only candidate, the interview panel and the person who made the coffee. He has bought a notebook, written ENQUIRY on the cover and underlined it twice. That remains the only thing in the notebook.
theory: Probably the cat.

title: The incident room
body:
The enquiry now has an incident room, in the corner of the living room behind the Christmas tree. The tree itself has been turned into an evidence board. Baubles mark persons of interest. Tinsel serves as the red string, and it ran out somewhere over the Indian Ocean while the editor was trying to connect the UK, Cebu and Sydney.

A new name has gone up at the top of the tree, where the star used to be. The editor explained his reasoning in a nine-minute voice note. The suspect is a known biscuit thief. He enters homes uninvited once a year. He has never once been charged. He has a beard, “which is what people grow when they have something to hide”. And he has a large sack, which nobody has ever been allowed to search.

The star has been moved to the bottom of the tree, where it is considered a witness.
theory: Santa. Possibly early reconnaissance.

title: The reindeer is questioned
body:
Following today’s front page, the editor interviewed the reindeer seen in reception, on the grounds that he is a known associate of the prime suspect. The interview took place over video. The reindeer joined on time with his camera on and a professional background, which the editor found suspicious in itself.

The reindeer said Santa does not touch biscuits until 24 December, for union reasons. The editor asked whether Santa might be freelancing. The reindeer said nobody freelances in December, then asked to be paid for his time in carrots. The editor wrote “CARROTS = BRIBE?” in his notebook and underlined it.

The interview ended when the editor’s screen froze with his mouth open and one finger raised, mid-accusation. He stayed like that for four minutes while the reindeer finished a sandwich.
theory: Santa, freelancing, with a reindeer as the getaway driver.

title: A search of the museum
body:
Acting on a hunch, the editor searched the museum in the spare room. Its one exhibit, the mug, is wearing a small Santa hat for its festive exhibition. The tin was not in the mug, under the mug, or under the hat.

On his hands and knees beneath the display table, the editor found two things: the remote control that went missing in 2023, and a single crumb. He identified it as shortbread, not mince pie, after tasting it, which he now accepts was not standard forensic procedure.

He sealed what was left of the crumb in a sandwich bag labelled EXHIBIT B. Then, overcome by the importance of the moment, he sneezed it out of the bag and into the Christmas tree. It is now a decoration.
theory: Somebody ate shortbread in the museum. The mince pies have motive.

title: A fingertip search
body:
The weekend gave the enquiry time for a full fingertip search of the house, combined, for efficiency, with putting up the rest of the Christmas decorations. It found three remote controls, a string of lights that only work when nobody is looking at them, and last year’s Secret Santa present, still wrapped, still from “???”.

The search covered the loft, the garage, under the tree, behind the sofa and inside the turkey, which is frozen and was therefore searched by knocking on it. It did not cover the desk. The editor explained that the desk is “where the work happens”, and that searching your own desk is what people do when they have lost something, which he hasn’t, because it was stolen, by Santa.

He then spent four minutes looking for his reading glasses, which were on his head, under a Santa hat, which he was also wearing.
theory: Santa. With help on the inside. Possibly the elves.

title: The only witness
body:
A breakthrough. In the drawer where the Christmas crackers live, the editor found a single shortbread finger, separated from the rest of the tin and living quietly among the paper hats since the spring.

The witness was brought to the incident room and placed on a saucer under the tree for questioning. It said nothing, which the editor took to be fear. He asked it gently where the others were. It said nothing. He leaned in and whispered, “Just point.” After a long silence, the shortbread finger pointed in the general direction of the study, the kitchen, the Christmas tree and about forty other things.

The editor thanked the witness for its time, noted that it was clearly in shock, and ate it. Asked later whether eating the only witness had been wise, he said it was “a judgement call” and “very nice, actually, a bit soft”.
theory: The witness was protecting someone. Someone with a beard.

title: Christmas cards
body:
To rattle the suspects, the editor sent each of them a Christmas card. Inside every one he wrote: “Season’s greetings. We know what you did.” He signed them “The Enquiry”, then added a kiss out of habit, which he says has undermined the tone somewhat.

Santa’s card came back marked “Not known at this address”, which the editor calls “exactly what a guilty man would say”. The cat’s card was found under the cat. The ceiling has not responded.

A card also arrived from Head Office. It reads: “Hope the team enjoyed the tin! Photos for the Christmas newsletter by the 20th, please.” The editor has propped it on the mantelpiece, facing the wall.
theory: Santa. The man has no fixed address. Think about it.

title: Exhibit A is measured
body:
Today’s front page reports a circular mark on the editor’s desk. The enquiry has measured it with a borrowed tape measure: nineteen centimetres across. The tin, according to the manufacturer’s website, which the editor has now read four times, is also nineteen centimetres across.

The editor called this “a very interesting coincidence” and wrote it down. He has ruled out the advent candle, which is square, and the Christmas pudding, which he ate in 2024 and still thinks about.

He has ordered tests on the mark. The tests involve licking a finger, touching the mark and saying “hmm”. Results are expected in the new year, after the January sales.
theory: The tin was on the desk, and somebody took it off the desk. Santa has been known to come down chimneys. The study does not have a chimney. Yet.

title: Surveillance
body:
Inspired by today’s picture desk, the editor has put the garden under surveillance, convinced that the robin on the fork is working for Santa. “Look at any Christmas card,” he told us. “Who’s always there? Who’s always watching?”

He watched it from the kitchen window for six hours, in a Santa hat, for cover. The robin ate a worm, looked at the editor and left.

A neighbour reports that their doorbell camera caught the editor at 14:20 holding up a sign that read “WE KNOW”. The robin did not respond. The neighbour has asked whether everything is all right at home. The editor assured them it is “an active enquiry”. The neighbour has since been added to the tree.
theory: Santa runs an intelligence network of garden birds.

title: The bait
body:
At lunchtime the editor set a trap for Santa: a mince pie and a glass of milk on a plate by the back door, on the theory that Santa might be tempted into an early visit. To make it look realistic, the editor took a bite out of the mince pie. Then another. Then he finished it, drank the milk and reset the trap with a satsuma, which nobody has ever been tempted by.

During a call with a client that afternoon, still in his reindeer jumper, he was told he was “sitting very tall today” and asked whether he had a new chair. He said it was the jumper, and that vertical stripes are very slimming. The jumper has horizontal stripes. The client let it go.
theory: Santa is too clever for mince pies. A satsuma will separate the professionals from the amateurs.

title: The Working Group
body:
The enquiry has set up a Working Group. Its only member is the editor. He has produced a RACI chart, in which he is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, and Terms of Reference that thank him warmly for agreeing to take part.

Its first meeting was also its Christmas party. The editor wore a paper crown, pulled a cracker against himself and lost. He ran a Secret Santa with himself, and was delighted with his present, which was a stapler from his own desk.

Under Any Other Business, he asked whether anyone else could hear a faint rattle when he typed. Nobody else could. Nobody else was there.
theory: Santa, possibly with an elf on the inside. Elves are small and good at shelves.

title: A police sketch
body:
With a weekend to fill, the editor has drawn a sketch of the suspect from the evidence gathered so far. He was aiming for Santa. He started with the beard, then decided the beard was a disguise and rubbed it out. He then rubbed out the hat for the same reason, and the sack, which he said was “circumstantial”.

What is left is a man in a Christmas jumper, seen from the chest up, looking pleased with himself. The editor has pinned it to the top of the tree and called it “a very typical face”. He has asked readers to look out for this man. Several have written in to say they see him most days.
theory: Santa in plain clothes. Possibly a jumper.

title: The tree is questioned
body:
Today’s gardening column reports that the houseplant has thrived since being moved six inches to the left during the spring clean. The houseplant was questioned for forty minutes, said nothing and is cleared. It has been watered by way of apology.

The Christmas tree was then questioned, on the grounds that it has been dropping needles all week, “a classic sign of nerves”. It said nothing either, but continued to drop needles throughout, which the editor read as a confession and the rest of us read as December.

The tree is now in custody, in its usual corner, with the presents. The editor has told it not to leave the country. It has been told this before.
theory: The tree is in on it. It has been standing over the presents all week like it owns them.

title: An anonymous letter
body:
The enquiry has received its first anonymous letter. It reads, in full: “Have you tried looking under things?”

The editor called this “a gift” and spent the afternoon looking under things. He looked under the sofa, the rug, the doormat and the cat. He looked under every present beneath the tree and shook several of them, one of which was his own and is now broken. He looked under the mistletoe, which was awkward because the cat was also there.

He did not look under anything on the desk. Asked why not, he said “those aren’t things, those are tools”, and that whoever wrote the letter had “clearly never worked in operations”.
theory: Whoever wrote the letter knows more than they’re saying. Possibly the ceiling.

title: The smart speaker gives evidence
body:
Today’s front page mentions a witness who heard a sound “broadly consistent with a custard cream”. We can now reveal that the witness is the smart speaker in the kitchen. It overheard a rattle from the study and, when the editor asked it to “play back what you heard”, played eleven hours of Christmas music.

Under further questioning, the speaker confirmed that it hears the rattle every time someone types an angry email. The editor asked how often that is. The speaker said, “Forty-one times this week.” The editor asked it to stop being dramatic. The speaker said, “Okay, playing more Christmas music,” and is still doing so. Nobody in the house can remember how to make it stop. The cat has left home.
theory: The rattle is a coded message from the North Pole.

title: Interrogation music
body:
To unsettle the suspects, the editor asked Enviro FM to play “interrogation music” in the incident room. The request line offered him something festive with a strong bass line. Within minutes, something on the desk began to buzz gently in time with the music, like a very small metal drum.

The editor joined in on the drum part with two pencils. He has asked us not to describe the dancing. In fairness, we couldn’t.
theory: Santa has bugged the study.

title: Payroll replies
body:
The reindeer has returned with a reference from Payroll (see front page) and is released without charge. The editor then turned his attention to Payroll, emailing to ask whether they had noticed “any unexplained shortbread” in this year’s figures, and, while he had them, whether there was any news on Christmas bonuses.

Payroll replied within the hour. There was no news on bonuses. They had not noticed any shortbread. They had noticed an expense claim from the editor in March for “office furniture (tartan)”, at a cost of £0.00, with the note “found it in the house, bargain”. They asked why he had submitted it. He said he “believes in transparency”. Payroll said they believe in fewer emails, especially in December.
theory: Payroll know something. Payroll always know something.

title: Customs
body:
International post has landed, and the editor met it at the border, convinced Santa had smuggled the tin out in the Diplomatic Pouch. Customs let him look through the scanner logs, on condition that he stopped asking about the pun they’re holding.

The logs were clean. No tins of any kind have crossed any border this December. Customs did add one note, which the editor read aloud on a call before he had properly understood it: “The only tartan item to appear on any of our screens this year is visible on the editor’s own video calls, at the very bottom of the picture.”

He has since redecorated the bottom of the picture with tinsel.
theory: An international smuggling ring, tartan division, run from a sleigh.

title: Corrections
body:
The enquiry wishes to correct the following. The cat mentioned on 1, 7 and 14 December is a cushion. The editor does not own a cat. He owns a cat-shaped cushion, a Christmas present from a relative, and he has been questioning it all month. The ceiling has asked to be taken off the tree. The robin did nothing wrong, although it does look at us in a certain way.

Finally, the team email the editor sent in March, “Exciting news re: my home office spring clean”, included a photograph captioned “my new tartan stand — game changer”. We regret that the enquiry did not read it at the time. Neither, it now turns out, did anyone else.
theory: Back to square one, which, the editor points out, is not the shape of the tin.

title: The Christmas crossword
body:
In a last attempt to draw out a confession, the editor set a Christmas crossword for all the remaining suspects. The answers were TIN, UNDER, LAPTOP, TARTAN, MARCH and YOU. He left it under the tree overnight, in case Santa felt guilty enough to fill it in.

In the morning it had been completed in the editor’s own handwriting, with a mince pie crumb on the corner. He believes the culprit has been forging his handwriting, which he calls “the obvious explanation”, and eating his mince pies, which he calls “frankly, the last straw”.

Head Office has emailed again. The newsletter goes out today. They are using a stock photo of a biscuit.
theory: Forgery. By a bearded professional.

title: The handover
body:
Exhausted, the editor handed the enquiry to the Cebu and Sydney desks for the night, along with forty pages of notes, the tinsel, the tree and the instruction “don’t touch anything”.

Cebu solved the case in four minutes, during a coffee break. Sydney, where it was thirty-one degrees and the Christmas lights were wilting, checked the answer in two minutes and added a smiley face. They left a single sticky note on the handover for the editor to find in the morning: “Ayaw kabalaka. Lift the laptop.”

The editor looked up the first two words, which mean “don’t worry”, found this so reassuring that he stopped reading, and went back to bed. He has since had the whole note printed on a Christmas mug as a motto for the new year. The mug is on the desk, next to the laptop, which he has not lifted.
theory: The overseas desks are toying with me. It’s the festive spirit. I respect it.

title: The findings deck
body:
With the enquiry due to report, the editor presented his findings at the all-staff Christmas call. He had prepared forty-seven slides. Slide one said “WHO?”. Slides two to forty-six were stock photos of Santa looking shifty. Slide forty-seven said “Questions?”, and there were several, mostly about why he looked so tall.

An independent witness (see front page) then asked him to tilt his camera down and show everyone his desk. What happened next is on the front page. The enquiry’s own notes record only “tartan??”, in very small writing, next to a doodle of a sleigh.
theory: Someone tall. Someone close. Someone with a beard, or presence.

title: The trap
body:
Tonight is the night. The editor has set his final trap for Santa beside the fireplace: a mince pie, a carrot for the reindeer, a glass of milk and a net made from the tinsel.

The trap needed one last thing, a biscuit, as bait. The editor searched the whole house for one, from the loft to the cracker drawer. There are no biscuits anywhere. “Odd,” he wrote in the notebook. “You’d think there’d be a biscuit somewhere.”

He then packed for the Christmas break. His packing list, left on the desk, reads: 1. Charger. 2. Notebook (ENQUIRY). 3. Laptop. 4. Find out why laptop is so heavy. 5. Lift the laptop (mug).
theory: Tonight, Santa. Tonight.

title: Findings of the enquiry
body:
The enquiry presents its findings. The Communal Tin was never stolen. During the spring clean in March it was placed under the editor’s laptop as a “stand”, claimed on expenses at £0.00, photographed for a team email and then completely forgotten. For nine months the editor looked noticeably taller on every call and accepted every compliment.

The enquiry finds the editor Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. He is sentenced to share the shortbread, as originally instructed, with colleagues in three countries. He proposed a Sharing Framework, and it was rejected. The shortbread will instead be divided equally among everyone who reads this paper, which by the enquiry’s calculations comes to roughly one crumb each. Delivery arrangements are under review by the Working Group, which is him.

Santa has received a full apology and, at his request, a carrot. So have the reindeer, the robin, the cushion, the ceiling, the tree, the houseplant, Payroll and the smart speaker, which is still playing Christmas music. The shortbread finger is owed an apology and cannot receive one. The case is closed. The laptop now rests on a stack of paperbacks, and the editor is, once again, average. Merry Christmas.
theory: Case closed. It was me. Merry Christmas.
